Like a switch flips only when I see the water and that long stretch of concrete...\n\nDoctor: Is your fear when driving on bridges related to the height of the bridge, or is it more about being over the water?\n\nPatient: Well, you know, I've thought about that quite a bit, actually. Just cars whipping past you at eighty miles an hour, and all that exhaust... it’s just a highway suspended over the water, really. \n\nAnd frankly, doctor, even if they did have a nice, wide pedestrian path with a sturdy railing, well, I'm eighty-six years old! My long-distance walking days are pretty much behind me. I keep my walks mostly confined to the paved paths at the botanical gardens, or maybe a slow stroll down the aisles at Publix if my hip isn't acting up too badly that day. \n\nNow, I suppose there are smaller footbridges here and there. Arthur and I used to go to this lovely little nature preserve over in Pinellas County, oh, this must have been back in the late eighties, and they had a wooden boardwalk with a little bridge over a tidal creek. We'd stand there and look for herons and egrets. But I haven't been there in... oh, decades, probably. Certainly not since this whole awful fear of the big bridges started. \n\nSo, to answer your question, I honestly couldn't tell you if I'd panic the same way on foot. I just haven't tried it. Though, I must admit, just picturing myself standing out there in the open air, on foot, with the wind blowing and the water right beneath my shoes... well, it does give me a bit of a shiver just thinking about it! But I haven't actually put it to the test. Just trying to get my car across is quite enough trouble for me to handle right now.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your fear on the bridge would decrease if you were in a car that was being driven by someone you completely trusted?\n\nPatient: Someone I completely trust... well, that’s a tricky thing to measure, isn't it? Because, I mean, take my daughter, for example. She is a wonderful driver. Very cautious, very alert. She drives a sensible little sedan, always keeps her hands at ten and two, never speeds, never looks at her telephone... I trust her completely with my life. I really do. If she's driving me to the grocery store or a doctor's appointment on this side of the bay, I don't feel an ounce of worry. \n\nBut the moment we approach one of those large bridges... well, even with her behind the wheel, I still get that awful, dreadful fluttering in my chest. I still have to squeeze my eyes shut. I remember one time, we were going over to Tampa for a Sunday matinee—this was before I started turning down those trips entirely, like I was telling you earlier—and she kept saying, \"Mom, it's fine, I've got it, just breathe.\" And I knew she had it! I knew she was perfectly capable and wasn't going to drive us off the edge or do anything foolish. But my body just didn't seem to care who was driving. \n\nAnd it was the same with Arthur. I trusted him implicitly, we were married for fifty-two years, but if we were up high over the water, I'd still feel that same terrible knot in my stomach. So... does the trust decrease the fear? I honestly couldn't say for sure. I don't think it's about the driver at all, really. It's just the bridge itself. It's the height, the open water, the concrete stretching on and on. Once we're up there, it doesn't matter if it's my daughter, or Arthur, or... or the Pope himself chauffeuring me across! I'm still going to be sitting there clutching the door handle and praying for it to be over. So I really don't know if having a trusted driver makes a lick of difference to the panic itself.\n\nDoctor: Do you experience the fear or panic when you're just thinking about driving on a bridge, before you even get on it?\n\nPatient: Oh, heavens, yes. Yes, I absolutely do. It’s almost worse sometimes, the anticipation of it! I don't even have to be in the car, doctor. I can just be sitting in my living room, drinking my morning tea, and if I know I have an appointment or an errand across the bay later that week... well, my stomach just ties itself into absolute knots. \n\nI mean, I know perfectly well that those bridges are safe. They’ve been standing there for years and years! You see all those commuters and delivery trucks zooming across them every single day, bless their hearts, just going about their business like it's nothing at all. And logically, in my head, I know the engineering is sound. But... well, when I just sit there and think about having to drive up that steep incline, and being suspended over all that endless open water... oh, my goodness, my heart starts racing just talking to you about it right now! \n\nThe fear I feel... it just feels so much bigger, so much more overwhelming than any actual danger there might be. I know the real danger is practically zero, I really do. I have a college degree, I am a rational woman! But my mind just takes that thought of the water and the height, and it spins it out of control until I'm pacing the floor, getting out my old paper maps, trying to figure out if I can take some ridiculous detour just to avoid it. It’s exhausting, really, how much time I spend just dreading the whole ordeal before I've even picked up my car keys...\n\nDoctor: Do you ever find yourself worrying about bridges when you're not driving or thinking about an upcoming trip that involves crossing a bridge?\n\nPatient: Well... no, not really. I mean, if I don't have a reason to cross one, they don't just pop into my head out of nowhere. I'm not sitting around worrying about bridges in the abstract, if that makes sense. \n\nMy days are usually quite quiet, you know. I have my routines. I get up, I make my tea, I check my email—my granddaughter set me up with a lovely tablet, so I can see pictures of the great-grandbabies—and I might do a little gardening if the humidity isn't too oppressive. I have a beautiful bougainvillea that needs constant pruning, though Arthur always used to say I was too aggressive with the shears. Anyway, my point is, my mind is usually occupied with the day-to-day things. What to make for dinner, when the mail is coming, whether I need to call the plumber about that slow drip in the guest bathroom... \n\nI don't just sit in my armchair and fret about the Sunshine Skyway for no reason. It's really only when I know I have to face one. Like, if I get an invitation to a luncheon over in St. Pete, or if my doctor refers me to a specialist in Tampa. That's when the dread starts creeping in. That's when I start looking at the calendar and thinking, \"Oh, dear, next Thursday I have to cross the water.\" And then, of course, the worrying takes over completely, like I was just saying. But if I'm just staying on my side of the bay, running my usual errands, going to my church group... no, the bridges don't bother me at all. They might as well not even exist, as far as my daily life is concerned. I just stay in my little bubble, and everything is perfectly fine.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever felt this kind of fear or panic when you were in a high place, but not on a bridge, such as on a balcony or a mountaintop?\n\nPatient: Well... no. No, I really haven't. It's funny you ask that, because people always assume it's just a fear of heights in general, don't they? They think, \"Oh, she's afraid of bridges, she must be afraid of tall buildings or airplanes or what have you.\" But it's not like that at all. \n\nI remember, oh, this must have been... well, Arthur and I took a trip out West for our fortieth anniversary. We went to the Grand Canyon. And let me tell you, you stand on the edge of that thing, and it is a sheer drop! A mile straight down! And I stood right there on the rim, looking out over all that magnificent red rock, and I felt completely fine. Awed, yes, but not terrified. Not that awful, clutching panic I get on the bridges. And we used to go to Atlanta sometimes to visit Arthur's sister, Margaret—she passed away a few years ago, bless her heart—but she lived in this beautiful high-rise condo on the twentieth floor. We'd sit out on her balcony, drinking iced tea, looking over the whole city, and it never bothered me one bit. \n\nSo it really isn't just being up high. It's... it's the combination, I think. It's the height, yes, but it's being trapped in the car, and the water underneath, and that feeling that you're just suspended out there with nowhere to go. If I'm on a balcony, I can step back inside. If I'm on a mountain, I'm on solid ground. But a bridge... well, a bridge is a different beast entirely. So, no, to answer your question, it's really just the bridges that do this to me.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced this kind of fear or panic when you were on a bridge, but not in a car, such as walking or biking?\n\nPatient: Well, now, that's an interesting question... walking or biking? Oh, heavens, I haven't been on a bicycle since Arthur and I lived in our first house over in Clearwater, and that must have been the late sixties! I had this lovely blue Schwinn with a white basket, and I used to ride it down to the corner market to get fresh bread. But no, I haven't ridden a bike in decades, certainly not across a bridge. My knees would never allow it these days anyway! \n\nAs for walking... you know, I really can't say. I just don't do it. The bridges around here, the big ones anyway, they aren't exactly meant for a nice afternoon stroll, are they? The Sunshine Skyway, the Howard Frankland... goodness, you'd have to be out of your mind to try walking across those with all those cars whizzing by at seventy miles an hour! There's no sidewalk, no pedestrian path, nothing of the sort. \n\nNow, there are some smaller bridges, I suppose, like the little drawbridges out by the beaches. Sometimes people fish off of those, or walk across to get to the restaurants on the other side. But I just don't have any reason to do that. If I'm going to the beach, which is rare enough these days with how crowded it gets and the parking being such a nightmare, I'm driving. Or rather, I'm having someone drive me, because I certainly wouldn't take myself over those drawbridges either! \n\nSo, I suppose the honest answer is that I just don't know if I'd panic walking across one, because I simply avoid them entirely. If I'm not in a car, I'm not on a bridge. It's just not something that comes up in my day-to-day life, you see. I stick to solid ground, my garden, my living room... places where I know my own two feet are safe and sound on the earth. Why tempt fate, I always say!\n\nDoctor: Would you feel the same level of fear if you were on a bridge but not driving, such as if you were a pedestrian?\n\nPatient: Well, like I was just saying... I really couldn't tell you for sure, because I just don't put myself in that situation. I mean, the very thought of being on a bridge, whether I'm behind the wheel or just walking on my own two feet... it just doesn't sit right with me. \n\nBut if I really think about it, if I try to imagine myself walking across, say, the Courtney Campbell Causeway... oh, heavens. I think it might actually be worse! Because when you're in a car, at least you have the metal around you, you know? You have the doors locked, the windows rolled up, the air conditioning running. You feel a little bit insulated from it all, even if you are terrified. But walking? Out there in the open air, with the wind whipping off the bay, and nothing between you and that dark water but a little concrete railing? Oh, my word, no. \n\nI remember once, years and years ago, Arthur and I were visiting his cousin in New York, and they wanted to walk across the Brooklyn Bridge. It's supposed to be this iconic thing to do, you know, very romantic. Well, I got about fifty feet onto that wooden walkway, and I looked down at the East River, and I just froze. I couldn't take another step. The wind was blowing my scarf every which way, the traffic was roaring underneath us, and I just felt so exposed, so vulnerable. Arthur had to practically carry me back to the Manhattan side. \n\nSo, yes, even though I don't do it nowadays, I imagine the fear would be just as bad, if not worse. Being a pedestrian doesn't make the bridge any shorter or the water any shallower, does it? You're still trapped out there, suspended in the air, and that's the part that really gets to me. It's that feeling of being completely at the mercy of this giant structure, with no quick way back to solid, reliable earth. So I just stay away. It's the only sensible thing to do at my age, really. Why put myself through that kind of torment when I have a perfectly lovely garden right here in my own backyard?\n\nDoctor: Would your fear of bridges be the same if you were on a boat or a ferry crossing under the bridge, rather than driving or walking on it?\n\nPatient: A boat? Oh, goodness me, a boat is an entirely different story. You know, Arthur—my late husband, I think I mentioned him earlier—he actually owned a little pontoon boat for a few years right after he retired from the firm. We used to take it out on Boca Ciega Bay on Sunday afternoons, just puttering around at our own pace, looking at the dolphins and the pelicans. We'd pack some sandwiches, maybe a little thermos of coffee... anyway, sometimes we'd go right under the John's Pass bridge, or even the bigger ones if we ventured out far enough toward the gulf. And looking up at it from underneath? Not a flutter of panic. Not one single flutter. Because on a boat, you're already right there on the water, you see? You aren't suspended up in the clouds, trapped in a vehicle high in the air. \n\nThe bridge itself isn't some sort of monster, it's just concrete and steel. And I know that! I really do. I sit in my living room and I tell myself, I know perfectly well those bridges have been there for years and years, and plenty of people cross them every single day. Goodness, you watch the traffic reports on the evening news and you see cars just packed bumper to bumper on them! Commuters, school buses, delivery trucks... they all get across just fine. So I know they aren't going to just crumble into the sea. I know the actual risk of something happening is practically zero. \n\nBut... oh, it's so hard to explain to someone who doesn't feel it... when I actually think about driving over all that open water, the fear just swells up inside my chest, and it feels so much bigger than the actual danger. It is completely out of proportion, I know it is! My rational mind tells me that everything is perfectly safe and ordinary, but the panic just completely takes over my body. It's terribly frustrating because I'm an educated woman, I have my bachelor's degree, I shouldn't be acting so silly about a simple piece of roadway. But the terror is just so overwhelming compared to the reality of the situation. It really is quite baffling when you stop and think about it, isn't it?\n\n[Instruction]\n- Ask about exactly ONE thing. Well, let me think about that... a specific type. No, no, I really wouldn't say it's limited to just one kind. You mentioned suspension bridges, and of course, those are simply terrifying all on their own. When I'm gripping that wheel, I'm not really thinking logically about shoulders or emergency lanes, I'm just thinking, \"Get me off this thing, get me back to solid ground.\"\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced this kind of fear or panic when you're a passenger in a car on a bridge, rather than the driver?\n\nPatient: Well, it’s... it’s a bit different when I’m in the passenger seat, though I wouldn't say it's exactly a pleasant ride. I still get that awful nervous flutter, and I usually have to close my eyes and just grip the door handle for dear life until we're over the hump. But I don't get quite that same level of sheer, blinding panic where I feel like I'm going to lose control of the vehicle, because, well, I'm not the one controlling it. \n\nBut you see, doctor, that has become a whole other problem in and of itself! Because I can only manage it if someone else is driving, I’ve actually started turning down things I really love doing. I've been missing gallery openings—there was a lovely watercolor exhibit just last week over in St. Pete that I completely skipped—and my regular birdwatching trips, which I’ve been going on since the late nineties. I’ve even found myself making excuses to turn down visits with my own daughter, unless someone else can drive me over the bridges. \n\nAnd I cannot even begin to tell you how much that embarrasses me. I am just absolutely mortified by it. Because my entire life, I’ve always been the one who planned everything and handled things myself! When my husband Arthur was alive, especially when his health started failing, I drove us everywhere. I managed the schedules, the trips, I was always so capable and independent. And now? Now I'm sitting at home missing out on the spring migration, or having to call up a friend and beg them to chauffeur me across a piece of concrete like I’m some sort of helpless invalid. It is just humiliating. So yes, being a passenger is the only way I can even endure going over them right now, but having to rely on others just to leave my side of the bay has turned my life completely upside down...\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had to walk on a bridge, and if so, did you experience the same level of fear or panic?\n\nPatient: Walk on a bridge? Oh, heavens, no. No, I certainly haven't done that. I mean, if you think about the bridges we have around here—the big ones, the ones that cause me all this grief—they aren't exactly meant for a Sunday stroll, are they? You'd have to be absolutely out of your mind to try and walk across the Howard Frankland! Just cars whipping past you at eighty miles an hour, and all that exhaust... it’s just a highway suspended over the water, really. \n\nAnd frankly, doctor, even if they did have a nice, wide pedestrian path with a sturdy railing, well, I'm eighty-six years old! My long-distance walking days are pretty much behind me. I keep my walks mostly confined to the paved paths at the botanical gardens, or maybe a slow stroll down the aisles at Publix if my hip isn't acting up too badly that day. \n\nNow, I suppose there are smaller footbridges here and there. Arthur and I used to go to this lovely little nature preserve over in Pinellas County, oh, this must have been back in the late eighties, and they had a wooden boardwalk with a little bridge over a tidal creek. We'd stand there and look for herons and egrets. But I haven't been there in... oh, decades, probably. Certainly not since this whole awful fear of the big bridges started. \n\nSo, to answer your question, I honestly couldn't tell you if I'd panic the same way on foot. I just haven't tried it. Though, I must admit, just picturing myself standing out there in the open air, on foot, with the wind blowing and the water right beneath my shoes... well, it does give me a bit of a shiver just thinking about it! But I haven't actually put it to the test. Just trying to get my car across is quite enough trouble for me to handle right now.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your fear on the bridge would decrease if you were in a car that was being driven by someone you completely trusted?\n\nPatient: Someone I completely trust... well, that’s a tricky thing to measure, isn't it? Because, I mean, take my daughter, for example. She is a wonderful driver. Very cautious, very alert. She drives a sensible little sedan, always keeps her hands at ten and two, never speeds, never looks at her telephone... I trust her completely with my life. I really do. If she's driving me to the grocery store or a doctor's appointment on this side of the bay, I don't feel an ounce of worry. \n\nBut the moment we approach one of those large bridges... well, even with her behind the wheel, I still get that awful, dreadful fluttering in my chest. Once we're up there, it doesn't matter if it's my daughter, or Arthur, or... or the Pope himself chauffeuring me across! I'm still going to be sitting there clutching the door handle and praying for it to be over. Yes, I absolutely do. It’s almost worse sometimes, the anticipation of it! I don't even have to be in the car, doctor. I can just be sitting in my living room, drinking my morning tea, and if I know I have an appointment or an errand across the bay later that week... well, my stomach just ties itself into absolute knots. \n\nI mean, I know perfectly well that those bridges are safe. They’ve been standing there for years and years! It's the height, yes, but it's being trapped in the car, and the water underneath, and that feeling that you're just suspended out there with nowhere to go. Well, now, that is exactly what it has come to these days, doctor. If someone else is driving, the fear is certainly still there—oh my, yes. I remember once, oh, it must have been five or six years ago, they were doing some sort of construction on the Sunshine Skyway—which is just a terrifying structure to begin with, frankly, all those cables and that steep incline, it looks like a roller coaster—and traffic was backed up for miles. I wasn't driving, thank goodness, my late husband Arthur was driving. He had this wonderful old Cadillac, rode like a dream, but we were just sitting there, inching along, and I remember thinking, \"Good heavens, if someone had a medical emergency up here, what on earth would they do?\" \n\nBut is that what's causing the fear now? The not being able to pull over? I'm honestly not certain. Because, you see, even if there were a wide shoulder, a perfectly safe place to pull off and put on the hazard lights... Even if it's two in the morning and there's not another soul on the road and I could just stop right in the middle lane if I wanted to—not that I ever would, of course, that's incredibly dangerous and illegal—but even if I could, I think I'd still be just as frantic to get to the other side. \n\nSo, I suppose the lack of a shoulder doesn't help matters, it certainly adds to the general unpleasantness of the situation, but I wouldn't say it's the root of the problem. Or maybe it is? It's just so hard to untangle all these feelings once that panic sets in. When I'm gripping that wheel, I'm not really thinking logically about shoulders or emergency lanes, I'm just thinking, \"Get me off this thing, get me back to solid ground.\"\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced this kind of fear or panic when you're a passenger in a car on a bridge, rather than the driver?\n\nPatient: Well, it’s... it’s a bit different when I’m in the passenger seat, though I wouldn't say it's exactly a pleasant ride. I still get that awful nervous flutter, and I usually have to close my eyes and just grip the door handle for dear life until we're over the hump. But I don't get quite that same level of sheer, blinding panic where I feel like I'm going to lose control of the vehicle, because, well, I'm not the one controlling it. \n\nBut you see, doctor, that has become a whole other problem in and of itself! Because I can only manage it if someone else is driving, I’ve actually started turning down things I really love doing. I've been missing gallery openings—there was a lovely watercolor exhibit just last week over in St. Pete that I completely skipped—and my regular birdwatching trips, which I’ve been going on since the late nineties. I’ve even found myself making excuses to turn down visits with my own daughter, unless someone else can drive me over the bridges. \n\nAnd I cannot even begin to tell you how much that embarrasses me. I am just absolutely mortified by it. Because my entire life, I’ve always been the one who planned everything and handled things myself! When my husband Arthur was alive, especially when his health started failing, I drove us everywhere. I managed the schedules, the trips, I was always so capable and independent. And now? Now I'm sitting at home missing out on the spring migration, or having to call up a friend and beg them to chauffeur me across a piece of concrete like I’m some sort of helpless invalid. It is just humiliating. So yes, being a passenger is the only way I can even endure going over them right now, but having to rely on others just to leave my side of the bay has turned my life completely upside down...\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had to walk on a bridge, and if so, did you experience the same level of fear or panic?\n\nPatient: Walk on a bridge? Oh, heavens, no. No, I certainly haven't done that. I mean, if you think about the bridges we have around here—the big ones, the ones that cause me all this grief—they aren't exactly meant for a Sunday stroll, are they? You'd have to be absolutely out of your mind to try and walk across the Howard Frankland! Just cars whipping past you at eighty miles an hour, and all that exhaust... it’s just a highway suspended over the water, really. \n\nAnd frankly, doctor, even if they did have a nice, wide pedestrian path with a sturdy railing, well, I'm eighty-six years old! Arthur and I used to go to this lovely little nature preserve over in Pinellas County, oh, this must have been back in the late eighties, and they had a wooden boardwalk with a little bridge over a tidal creek. We'd stand there and look for herons and egrets. But I haven't been there in... oh, decades, probably. Certainly not since this whole awful fear of the big bridges started. \n\nSo, to answer your question, I honestly couldn't tell you if I'd panic the same way on foot. I just haven't tried it. But I haven't actually put it to the test. Just trying to get my car across is quite enough trouble for me to handle right now.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your fear on the bridge would decrease if you were in a car that was being driven by someone you completely trusted?\n\nPatient: Someone I completely trust... well, that’s a tricky thing to measure, isn't it? Because, I mean, take my daughter, for example. She is a wonderful driver. Very cautious, very alert. She drives a sensible little sedan, always keeps her hands at ten and two, never speeds, never looks at her telephone... I trust her completely with my life. I really do. If she's driving me to the grocery store or a doctor's appointment on this side of the bay, I don't feel an ounce of worry. \n\nBut the moment we approach one of those large bridges... well, even with her behind the wheel, I still get that awful, dreadful fluttering in my chest. I still have to squeeze my eyes shut. I knew she was perfectly capable and wasn't going to drive us off the edge or do anything foolish. But my body just didn't seem to care who was driving. \n\nAnd it was the same with Arthur. I trusted him implicitly, we were married for fifty-two years, but if we were up high over the water, I'd still feel that same terrible knot in my stomach. So... does the trust decrease the fear? I honestly couldn't say for sure. I don't think it's about the driver at all, really. It's just the bridge itself. It's the height, the open water, the concrete stretching on and on. Once we're up there, it doesn't matter if it's my daughter, or Arthur, or... or the Pope himself chauffeuring me across! I'm still going to be sitting there clutching the door handle and praying for it to be over. So I really don't know if having a trusted driver makes a lick of difference to the panic itself.\n\nDoctor: Do you experience the fear or panic when you're just thinking about driving on a bridge, before you even get on it?\n\nPatient: Oh, heavens, yes. Yes, I absolutely do. It’s almost worse sometimes, the anticipation of it! I don't even have to be in the car, doctor. I can just be sitting in my living room, drinking my morning tea, and if I know I have an appointment or an errand across the bay later that week... well, my stomach just ties itself into absolute knots. \n\nI mean, I know perfectly well that those bridges are safe. They’ve been standing there for years and years! You see all those commuters and delivery trucks zooming across them every single day, bless their hearts, just going about their business like it's nothing at all. And logically, in my head, I know the engineering is sound. But... well, when I just sit there and think about having to drive up that steep incline, and being suspended over all that endless open water... oh, my goodness, my heart starts racing just talking to you about it right now! \n\nThe fear I feel... it just feels so much bigger, so much more overwhelming than any actual danger there might be. I know the real danger is practically zero, I really do. I have a college degree, I am a rational woman! But my mind just takes that thought of the water and the height, and it spins it out of control until I'm pacing the floor, getting out my old paper maps, trying to figure out if I can take some ridiculous detour just to avoid it. I'm not sitting around worrying about bridges in the abstract, if that makes sense. \n\nMy days are usually quite quiet, you know. I have my routines. I get up, I make my tea, I check my email—my granddaughter set me up with a lovely tablet, so I can see pictures of the great-grandbabies—and I might do a little gardening if the humidity isn't too oppressive. I have a beautiful bougainvillea that needs constant pruning, though Arthur always used to say I was too aggressive with the shears. What to make for dinner, when the mail is coming, whether I need to call the plumber about that slow drip in the guest bathroom... \n\nI don't just sit in my armchair and fret about the Sunshine Skyway for no reason. They might as well not even exist, as far as my daily life is concerned. But being a passenger is the only way I can endure it at all, and I find myself avoiding so much of my life just to keep from having to ask for that help.
